html:
A violent eruption of Mount Tarawera, near Rotorua on New Zealand's North Island, in the early hours of 10 June 1886. It killed about 120 people and destroyed the Pink and White Terraces, then the country's most famous natural wonder.

The eruption began around 2 in the morning and lasted about six hours. A rift opened along the mountain and beyond it, through Lake Rotomahana, throwing up ash, rock and mud. The Māori villages of Te Wairoa, Moura and Te Ariki were buried, and most of those who died were Māori, many of them of the Tūhourangi people.

The Pink and White Terraces were great staircases of silica built up by hot springs on the shore of Lake Rotomahana. Tourists had come from around the world to see them, guided and hosted by the Tūhourangi of Te Wairoa, whose living was ruined. It was the largest and deadliest eruption in New Zealand in the past 500 years. The Waimangu valley of hot springs formed in its wake. Compare Krakatoa three years earlier. See New Zealand.
